nameStory: Common duckweed gets its name from being a favorite food of ducks and other waterfowl. These tiny floating plants are so beloved by ducks that dense mats of duckweed can disappear overnight when a flock discovers them. The 'weed' part refers to how quickly it spreads across ponds and slow-moving water.
description: Common duckweed is one of the world's smallest flowering plants, looking like tiny green oval discs floating on water surfaces. Each individual plant is only about the size of your pinky nail, with a single root dangling beneath like a miniature anchor. Though small individually, duckweed often forms dense green carpets that can cover entire ponds or quiet stream sections. These floating mats can be so thick they look like you could walk across them.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense floating mats on water surface that feel spongy when you gently press them with a stick - the plants give way but spring back

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Tiny oval or round green discs, each about 1/8 to 1/4 inch across, smooth to the touch and bright green on top with a single root hanging underneath

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Flowers are extremely rare and tiny - you'd need a magnifying glass to see them - most reproduction happens when plants simply split apart

idTips.label: Root System
idTips.description: Each plant has just one thin white root dangling 1-2 inches below the floating leaf, visible when you lift plants from water

habitat: Found floating on quiet freshwater surfaces throughout New England - ponds, slow streams, marshes, and even roadside ditches. Prefers nutrient-rich water in full sun to partial shade, often abundant in farm ponds and suburban water features. Thrives in still or very slow-moving water where it won't be swept away by currents.

seasonality.spring: Begins growing rapidly as water warms, spreading quickly across pond surfaces. This is when you'll see the fastest growth and brightest green color.
seasonality.summer: Peak abundance with thick floating mats covering large areas of suitable habitat. Plants are actively reproducing by splitting apart to form new individuals.
seasonality.fall: Growth slows and some plants may sink to pond bottoms as temperatures drop. Mats become less dense and plants may appear slightly yellowed.
seasonality.winter: Most plants die back or remain dormant underwater as hardy buds, though some may persist under ice in protected spots until spring returns.

funFact: Common duckweed is one of the fastest-growing plants on Earth - under perfect conditions, it can double its population every 16 hours, meaning a single plant could theoretically cover an acre of water in just one month!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other duckweed species, but common duckweed has just one root per plant while ivy-leaved duckweed is more translucent and turion duckweed has multiple roots. Remember: one root = common duckweed.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'weed,' duckweed is actually beneficial - it produces more protein per acre than soybeans and helps clean polluted water by absorbing excess nutrients. It's also completely edible and nutritious for humans, though most people prefer to leave it for the ducks.
compareHints: Common duckweed differs from its relatives by having exactly one root per plant and opaque green leaves. Ivy-leaved duckweed is more see-through and often stays slightly submerged, while turion duckweed has 2-5 roots per plant. Common duckweed also tends to form the densest, most continuous floating mats of the three species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike Common Duckweed which floats on the surface with round fronds, Ivy-leaved Duckweed lives underwater with three-lobed fronds that stay connected in chains.
Turion duckweed looks almost identical to common duckweed, but produces the distinctive sinking turions that common duckweed cannot make.
